column3: One review for every teammate, plus the five behavior questions about yourself. A three-person group means two teammate blocks; a four-person group means three.
column6: Every teammate reviewed and the self-section done.
column9: One teammate skipped, or the self-section left blank.

column3: The Continue and Start/Stop answers. Each names a concrete behavior, its effect on the work, and something the person could actually do. This is the heart of the assignment.
column6: Every answer names a specific behavior and its effect, and the Start/Stop answers say what to do instead.
column9: Most answers are concrete; one or two are generic praise or vague criticism.
column12: About half the answers could apply to any teammate on any project.
column15: Answers are one-liners or empty compliments with nothing to act on.

column3: Names something the person did that GitHub would not show: unblocking someone, running a meeting, keeping the board current, explaining something, defusing a disagreement. Saying honestly that you cannot think of anything counts as an answer.
column6: Identifies real non-code contribution, or gives an honest and specific account of why there was none.
column9: Answers the question but restates code work already visible in the repo.

column3: The five behavior questions about yourself plus the written self-reflection. Graded on whether you engaged with it, not on how highly you rated yourself.
column6: Self-ratings completed and the reflection names a real contribution and a real shortfall.
column9: Completed but the reflection is generic, or claims no shortfall at all.

column3: Critiques behavior and its effect on the work rather than the person's character. Written the way you would want a teammate to write about you.
column9: Drifts into personal characterization, or is so hedged it says nothing.
column12: Insulting, or targets the person rather than the work.
